passages.subject: cma
passages.text: ABC is a two-stage system: Resources →(resource cost driver)→ Activities/cost pools →(activity cost driver)→ Cost objects. It was born from rising overheads (automation), stiffer competition, greater product diversity and cheaper IT — which made the traditional volume-based OAR (DLH/MH) inaccurate. One core formula runs every sum: Activity Cost Driver Rate = Total Cost of Activity ÷ Activity Driver, computed separately for each activity. Activities sit in a four-level hierarchy — Unit, Batch, Product, Facility (mnemonic U-B-P-F) — and only the first three trace to products. ABC generates information; ABM uses it to manage costs; ABB reverses the ABC process to build budgets from planned activity levels.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Activity Based Costing does not push overheads straight onto products. It routes them through the activities that actually consume resources, in two stages: Stage 1 — Resources →( Resource Cost Driver )→ Activities / Cost Pools: assign cost to the activity. Stage 2 — Activities / Cost Pools →( Activity Cost Driver )→ Cost Objects: assign cost to the product or customer. Why ABC was born: rising overheads (automation) + rising competition + rising product diversity + falling IT cost. Together these made the traditional volume-based overhead absorption rate (on direct labour hours or machine hours) inaccurate. Chapter mnemonic — "RUB CD SLAB": Resource → Use By activity; Cost pool; Driver; Stages; Levels (hierarchy); ABM; Budgeting (ABB). Applications flow in one direction: ABC is a decision-making tool → ABM manages costs with the information → ABB budgets with it (and is the reverse of A

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Activity Based Costing (CIMA): Tracing resource consumption and costing final outputs. Resources are assigned to activities; activities are assigned to cost objects based on consumption estimates; and cost drivers attach cost to outputs . Reproduce this three-step chain verbatim in definition questions. The Institute's version says the same thing from the other side: ABC assigns cost to activities, not directly to products — resources → activities → cost objects, via cost drivers. It is not simply another absorption base; it is a distinct two-stage philosophy. Activity: An event that incurs cost. An activity cuts across departments — it is not the same thing as a cost centre. Cost object: Any item for which cost measurement is required. It is not limited to a product — a customer or a distribution channel is equally a cost object. Cost pool / bucket: A group of cost items sharing the sam

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: e cause-and-effect relationship , for example machine set-up. A cost pool is not a cost centre or a department. Cost driver: A factor causing a change in the cost of an activity. Never use the term generically — there are two: a Resource Cost Driver (quantity of resources consumed by an activity; assigns resource cost to the activity — Stage 1) and an Activity Cost Driver (frequency or intensity of demand placed by cost objects; assigns activity cost to the cost object — Stage 2). Two more terms carry marks on their own: Term Crisp meaning Trap / keyword --- --- --- VA activity Indispensable; the customer is willing to pay for it, e.g. furniture polishing — NVA activity Not valued by the customer; does not improve quality but does affect cost, e.g. material movement, machine set-up Machine set-up is NVA even though it is "necessary" — frequently tested ABM Use of ABC as a costing tool to

passages.text: Four levels (Cooper, 1990), mnemonic U-B-P-F: # Level Varies with Examples --- --- --- --- 1 Unit level Number of units produced Indirect material; inspecting every item 2 Batch level Number of batches (fixed per batch) Set-up; purchase order per batch 3 Product level Existence of the product line Design, specification, drawings 4 Facility level Nothing — common/joint to all products, not traceable Building maintenance, security The classic discrimination test: "inspect every item" is unit level; "inspect the first item of every batch" is batch level. Machine set-up is batch level — and is an NVA activity. Traditional costing based on DLH or MH under-costs low-volume/complex products and over-costs high-volume/simple products, because it ignores the non-volume drivers (batches, set-ups, orders) that those products actually consume. Stated the other way round: under-costed means ABC cost

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: is greater than traditional cost; over-costed means traditional cost is greater than ABC cost. ABC differs from traditional absorption costing on six points: overheads go to activities/cost pools rather than cost centres; multiple activity-wise rates rather than a single or departmental rate; cost drivers rather than time alone; realistic rather than unrealistic allocation; cost objects (customer/product/service) rather than cost units only; and it aids cost control by letting NVA activities be eliminated, whereas cost centres cannot be eliminated.

passages.subject: cma
passages.section: When ABC works — and when it does not
passages.text: Suitable when overheads are high and form a significant % of total cost; the product range is wide and diverse; significant non-volume-related activities (material handling, inspection, set-up) exist; and competition is stiff, so accurate cost and market-based pricing matter. Unsuitable / limitations — more expensive than traditional costing; not helpful for small organisations; may not suit organisations with limited or few products; and selecting the most suitable cost driver can be difficult. Advantages — more accurate costing, logical overhead allocation, better pricing, focus on unit cost, identification of NVA activities for cost reduction, usefulness for multi-product firms, and it highlights problem areas. Counts worth memorising: steps in ABC = 5 · requirements for implementation = 5 · ABM analyses = 3 (cost driver, activity VA/NVA, performance) · ABM in business = 4 (cost reduc

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Four words the examiner swaps deliberately: Budget is the document/target, Budgeting is the process, Forecast is a flexible probable assessment that feeds the budget, and Budgetary Control is the whole system — establish, compare, correct, fix responsibility. The key (principal) budget factor is identified FIRST; it sets the ceiling for every other budget. Usually sales demand, but it can be material, labour, power, capital or regulation. Types run CAP-FUN-MASTER-PERIOD-Z-P-R: capacity-wise (Fixed/Flexible), function-wise (15 functional budgets), Master Budget (= Budgeted P&L + Budgeted B/S), period-wise, plus ZBB, Performance Budgeting and the budget ratios. Fixed budget = ONE activity level, static. Flexible budget = recast at multiple levels, which first requires splitting semi-variable costs by the High-Low method — never extrapolate a single recovery rate to another level. Six budget ratios, all multiplied by 100, all favourable at 100% or more. Cash Budget is prepared LAST; COGS Budget = Production Cost Budget ± finished-goods stock adjustment.

passages.subject: cma
passages.section: The four terms and the budgeting flow
passages.text: Half the marks in a theory question here are lost to vocabulary. Four terms sit on a ladder from narrowest to broadest: Budget (a document/target) → Budgeting (the process that produces it) → Forecast (a flexible probable assessment that feeds into a budget) → Budgetary Control (the whole system). Budget (CIMA): A financial and/or quantitative statement, prepared and approved prior to a defined period of time , of the policy to be pursued during that period for the purpose of attaining a given objective. It is a document, a target — not the process. Budgetary Control (CIMA): The establishment of budgets + continuous comparison of actual with budgeted results + corrective action or revision . It is a system: establish, compare, revise, and fix responsibility. The broadest umbrella term of the four. Key / Principal Budget Factor: The factor that limits the total activity of the organisatio

passages.subject: cma
passages.section: The four terms and the budgeting flow
passages.text: n. Usually one or two factors bind — most commonly sales demand , but it can equally be material, labour, power, capital or government regulation. It must be identified first , because it sets the ceiling for every other functional budget. Two more pieces of vocabulary complete the set. The Budget Manual (CIMA) is the document setting out the responsibilities, routine, and the forms and records required for budgetary control — a procedure/guideline document, never the budget itself. The Budget Period is the time span a budget covers, and it is decided by the Budget Committee. Once the key factor is fixed, the budgets are built in a strict order: Key factor identified — sets the ceiling for everything below → Sales Budget — usually the starting point of the exercise → Production Budget → Material, Labour and Overhead Budgets → Production Cost Budget → (± finished-goods stock) → COGS Budge

CIMA defines the Master Budget as the summary budget incorporating all the functional budgets, finally approved, adopted and emplo

Every functional budget is only a subsidiary "schedule" to it. Four functional budgets attract nearly all the marks, and each has one rule that decides the answer: Budget Contents Key rule --- --- --- Production Cost Budget Material + Labour + Manufacturing expenses NO adjustment for finished-goods opening/closing stock Cost of Goods Sold Budget Production cost ± finished-goods stock Add opening FG, less closing FG — without this it is merely the Production Cost Budget Capital Expenditure Budget Planned outlay on fixed assets Long period, strict management control; feeds the Cash Budget Cash Budget Receipts and disbursements planning Prepared LAST among functional budgets — depends on all other budgets plus capital expenditure and financing Two smaller distincti

passages.text: ons worth a mark each: the Purchases Budget is the wider concept (it covers all items), with the Materials Budget only a part of it; and the Selling Cost Budget has a genuine anomaly — heavy selling and promotion spend may be needed exactly when sales are falling (pushing the cost-to-sales percentage up), and the benefit of one year's promotion may spill into subsequent years, so a stable cost-to-sales ratio is hard to fix.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Fixed Budget (CIMA): A budget designed to remain unchanged irrespective of the level of activity actually attained — a static budget, built for ONE activity level. Flexible Budget (CIMA): A budget which, by recognising the difference between fixed, variable and semi-variable cost behaviour, is designed to change in relation to the level of activity attained . Effectively a series of static budgets at different levels. Fixed Budget Flexible Budget --- --- --- Purpose Cost control at ONE activity level Cost/profit ascertainment at MULTIPLE activity levels Suitable when Stable, non-seasonal demand with no external impact; NOT suitable if conditions change Seasonal business, new venture, make-to-order, fashion-driven Prerequisite — A standard costing system, plus segregation of semi-variable costs The exception students miss: fixed budgets are still used by many service companies and by some

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: administrative functions of manufacturing companies — purchasing, engineering, accounting — even though a fixed budget is generally unsuitable for a dynamic business. Before a flexible budget can be recast at all, every semi-variable cost must be split into its fixed and variable elements by the High-Low method. Skip this and the flexible budget figures are simply wrong. High-Low method — splitting a semi-variable cost: \text{Variable cost per unit} = \frac{\text{Cost at higher activity} - \text{Cost at lower activity}}{\text{Higher output} - \text{Lower output}} \text{Fixed cost element} = \text{Total cost at a level} - (\text{Variable cost per unit} \times \text{output at that level}) \text{Total cost at new level} = \text{Fixed cost} + (\text{Variable cost per unit} \times \text{new output}) The classic trap (Illustration 1 pattern): taking a single recovery rate computed at one acti

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: vity level — say 70% — and applying it to estimate cost at another level — say 80% — gives a wrong, inflated figure. Fixed cost does not scale, so you must build a flexible budget rather than extrapolate a rate.

passages.text: Production and material budgets: \text{Production (units)} = \text{Budgeted Sales} + \text{Desired Closing Stock} - \text{Opening Stock} \text{Raw material consumption} = \text{Units to be produced} \times \text{Material required per unit} \text{Raw material purchase (qty)} = \text{Material for production} + \text{Desired Closing Stock} - \text{Opening Stock} Purchase quantity × rate gives the purchase value — the figure the Material Purchase Budget actually reports. Labour and factory overhead: \text{Number of workers required} = \frac{\text{Total budgeted hours}}{\text{Hours available per worker}} \text{Factory OH recovery rate} = \frac{\text{Total factory overhead}}{\text{Total budgeted direct labour hours}} Wages = number of workers × wage rate. A worked recovery rate from the source: ₹1,18,000 ÷ 1,18,000 hours = ₹1 per hour. Sales-mix budgeting: \text{Desired Contribution} = \text{F

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Zero Base Budgeting (ZBB): A technique in which each cost element is justified from a zero base , irrespective of its history. Also known as Priority-based Budgeting . Decision Package: a programme or activity described together with a cost-benefit analysis , ranked by priority. ZBB — four stages: Identify Decision Package → Evaluate → Rank by priority → Allocate resources. Corporate scope: best for discretionary costs — R&D, training, advertising — not for all costs. Non-corporate scope: government and not-for-profit entities, where it justifies social-programme spend. Contrast with traditional (incremental) budgeting: ZBB starts from zero, is decision-oriented, and places responsibility on the unit manager; traditional budgeting starts from last year's figure ± an adjustment, is accounting-oriented, and is decided by top management. Performance Budgeting (PB) correlates financial input

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: s with physical or functional outputs, and is synonymous with responsibility accounting. Its sequence — the ARC order — is Functions → Programme → Activity → Project. Against traditional budgeting, the contrast is one of focus: traditional budgeting looks at the object of expenditure (salaries, rent), while PB looks at function, programme and activity, and at the output. passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Mnemonic SING-R: System choice → Integrated (single book) or Non-integrated (Cost Ledger Control system) → General Ledger Adjustment A/c drives non-integrated → Reconciliation (only if non-integrated). Non-integrated keeps a separate Cost Ledger plus Stores, WIP/Job and Finished Goods subsidiary ledgers, run through 11 control accounts — and two profits are struck independently, so reconciliation is mandatory. The Cost Ledger Control A/c (General Ledger Adjustment A/c) completes the double entry: expenditure is credited to it and sales are debited to it — the opposite of intuition, and an MCQ favourite. Integrated (integral) accounting keeps ONE set of books; the CLC A/c is replaced by real accounts — Bank, Debtors, Creditors, Provision for Depreciation, Fixed Assets, Share Capital — so a single profit figure emerges and no reconciliation is needed. Profits differ for four reasons: items in only one set of books (purely financial items, notional charges), and the same item treated differently (stock valuation, depreciation method, over/under absorption) — reconcile via a statement or a Memorandum Reconciliation A/c.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: This chapter is about ledger architecture, not about a costing method. It answers one question: are the cost records and the financial records kept in one set of books, or two? Everything else follows from that single choice. S ystem choice — decide how cost and financial records relate. IN tegrated (single book) or N on-integrated (Cost Ledger Control system). G eneral Ledger Adjustment A/c drives the non-integrated system. R econciliation — required only if non-integrated. The cost flow is identical in both systems: Material → WIP → Finished Goods → Cost of Sales → Costing P&L. Only the "outside world" side of each entry changes. Cost Accounting System: Decides whether cost and financial records are integrated or separate . It is about ledger architecture, not about the costing method (job/process) used. passages.subject: cma
passages.text: A non-integrated system maintains separate ledgers for cost and financial accounts — it is also called the Cost Ledger A/c System or Cost Control System. The cost accounts restrict themselves to product/service items only; they exclude interest, bad debts and non-trading income. At its centre is the Cost Ledger — the principal ledger of the cost department, holding impersonal accounts and made self-balancing through control accounts. (ICAI spells this "principle" ledger; retain the ICAI wording in answers.) Cost Ledger Control A/c (General Ledger Adjustment A/c): The account that completes the double entry in a non-integrated system. Expenditure is credited to it and sales are debited to it — the opposite of intuition, and an MCQ favourite. Three subsidiary ledgers sit under the Cost Ledger: - Stores Ledger — one account per item of stores, carrying quantity and value. Item-wise; it is n

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: ot the aggregate Stores Ledger Control A/c. - WIP / Job Ledger — accounts of unfinished jobs or processes. The total of all job account balances equals the WIP Control A/c balance. - Finished Goods Ledger — one account per finished item. On completion: credit WIP Ledger, debit FG Ledger. Because the cost books deliberately exclude purely financial items and all balance-sheet items, a non-integrated system has fewer accounts than the financial books — and everything excluded is represented by that one account, the Cost Ledger Control A/c. The 11 control accounts, in flow order: CLC (GLA) → Stores → Wages → Manufacturing/Production OH → WIP → Admin OH → Finished Goods → S&D OH → Cost of Sales → Costing P&L → OH Adjustment (optional).

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Integrated (Integral) Accounting System: Cost and financial accounts kept in ONE set of books . It removes the need for reconciliation — not the need for costing information itself. Subsidiary ledgers (Stores, Stock, Job, Customers', Purchase) still exist. The CLC A/c disappears and real accounts take its place: Bank, Receivables (Debtors), Payables (Creditors), Provision for Depreciation, Fixed Assets, Share Capital. There is no notional or control substitute — complete balance-sheet detail is maintained. Transaction Entry --- --- Material purchased Stores Ledger Control A/c Dr. · To Creditors / Bank A/c Wages paid Wages Control A/c Dr. · To Bank A/c Overheads incurred OH Control A/c Dr. · To Bank A/c Sales Debtors / Bank A/c Dr. · To Sales A/c Receipts from debtors Bank A/c Dr. · To Debtors A/c Payments to creditors Creditors A/c Dr. · To Bank A/c Rest of flow: WIP → FG → Cost of Sales

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: This is largely an entries-based chapter, but a handful of figures are computed — and two of them are the classic "find the missing figure" balancing exercises. Overhead recovery rate: \text{OH Recovery Rate} = \frac{\text{Budgeted Overhead}}{\text{Budgeted Direct Labour Hours}} For example, ₹6,75,000 ÷ 4,50,000 hrs = ₹1.50 per hour. Direct wage rate per hour: \text{Direct Wage Rate per Hour} = \frac{\text{Direct Labour Cost on WIP}}{\text{Direct Labour Hours on WIP}} For example, ₹3,000 ÷ 1,200 = ₹2.50. Under / over absorption of overhead: \text{Under-absorption} = \text{Actual (Incurred)} - \text{Applied (Recovered)} \text{Over-absorption} = \text{Applied (Recovered)} - \text{Actual (Incurred)} Under-absorption arises when Incurred exceeds Recovered → debit Costing P&L / OH Adjustment A/c. Over-absorption arises when Recovered exceeds Incurred → credit Costing P&L / OH Adjustment A/c.

passages.subject: cma
passages.section: Reconciliation of costing and financial profit
passages.text: Reconciliation is needed only in a non-integrated system, because two profits are struck independently. The procedure has three steps: (1) ascertain the financial profit, (2) ascertain the cost profit, (3) reconcile the two — a procedure that parallels a bank reconciliation statement. It is done either through a Reconciliation Statement or a Memorandum Reconciliation A/c. Memorandum Reconciliation A/c: A non-ledger working used to reconcile costing profit with financial profit. It is NOT part of the double entry — never post it in a way that affects other balances. Profits differ for four reasons, in two families. Reasons 1 and 2 are items that appear in only one set of books. Reasons 3 and 4 are the same item treated on a different basis or by a different method. Notional Expenses: Imputed costs that appear in the cost accounts only , with no cash outflow: notional rent on owned premise

Expenses: interest on loans/mortgages, share and debenture issue expenses and discount, capital losses (uninsured fire loss), loss on sale of fixed assets or investments, income tax, donations, subscriptions, share transfer office expenses. passages.subject: cma
passages.text: One ladder runs the whole chapter — PWCOP-COGS-COS-P: DM+DL+DE = Prime Cost, +Factory OH = Gross Works Cost, ±WIP = Works Cost, then COP, COGS, Cost of Sales and Profit. Four cost heads (Prime Cost, Cost of Production, COGS, Cost of Sales) built on a functional classification: Production, Administration, Selling, Distribution, R&D. Three stock adjustments at three different points — RM before Prime Cost, WIP between Gross Works Cost and Works Cost, FG between COP and COGS. Never mix up placement. Two packing points and a two-way admin split: Primary packing and production-related Admin OH go into COP; Secondary packing and general Admin OH go into COS. Interest and finance cost is excluded from COP and shown as a separate line in COS; abnormal costs, penalties, fines, damages and demurrage are excluded from the cost sheet entirely.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: A cost sheet is one continuous build-up, and almost every question in this chapter is a test of whether you can climb the ladder in the right order and drop each item on the right rung. Memory hook — PWCOP-COGS-COS-P: Prime → Works → COP → COGS → COS → Profit. DM + DL + DE = Prime Cost + Factory OH = Gross Works Cost ± Opening/Closing WIP = Factory / Works Cost + QC + R&D (process) + Admin OH (production) − Credit for Recoveries (scrap/by-product) + Primary Packing = Cost of Production ± Opening/Closing FG = Cost of Goods Sold + Admin OH (General) + Selling OH + Secondary Packing + Distribution OH (interest on a separate line) = Cost of Sales Sales − Cost of Sales = Profit The ladder rests on a functional classification — Production, Administration, Selling, Distribution and R&D. That is the usual basis of a cost sheet, though other classifications are allowed if the user of the statemen

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: t needs them. There are four cost heads (Prime Cost, Cost of Production, COGS, Cost of Sales) and three stock-adjustment points. Material consumed is the first thing to get right, because the figure given in a question is usually purchases, not consumption: Materials consumed: \text{Materials Consumed} = \text{Opening RM} + \text{Purchases} - \text{Closing RM} Add freight inward and procurement insurance to material cost; deduct trade discount; add duty or tax only if ITC is not available. Prime Cost and Works Cost: \text{Prime Cost} = \text{Direct Material} + \text{Direct Employee (Labour)} + \text{Direct Expenses} \text{Gross Works Cost} = \text{Prime Cost} + \text{Factory / Works OH} \text{Works Cost} = \text{Gross Works Cost} + \text{Opening WIP} - \text{Closing WIP} WIP is valued at percentage completion per cost element, and the WIP adjustment sits between Gross Works Cost and Work

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Cost sheet / cost statement: A document presenting detailed cost information, typically on a functional basis. Other classifications are also permitted depending on what the user of the statement needs. Direct Material Cost: The cost of material consumed , not material purchased. Taken net of trade discount, and excluding GST on which ITC has been availed. Direct Expenses: Directly traceable expenses that are neither material nor labour — royalty, hire of equipment taken for a specific job, a special frame made for an order, and the amortised cost of moulds and patterns. Quality Control Cost: Resources devoted to quality-control procedures. Laboratory staff salary and testing costs are QC cost — not Works OH and not R&D. QC is added at the COP stage. Abnormal cost: A cost that is both material and quantifiable and unusual in nature — for example pandemic or lockdown costs. Excluded from

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Four different fates await an "unusual" item, and the exam turns on telling them apart — excluded, reduced, deducted, or shown separately. Excluded from the cost sheet entirely: abnormal costs (material and quantifiable, e.g. COVID/lockdown); penalty, fine, damages, demurrage; ITC-eligible GST and duties on raw material. Reduced, not shown as income: subsidy, grant or incentive received or receivable — reduced from the cost object. Deducted from COP, not added as income: credit for recoveries (realisable value of scrap and waste) and the NRV of by-products. Separate line item, not merged: interest and other finance costs — shown distinctly at the COS stage; alternatively they may be excluded from COS and shown separately in the P&L. Three further carve-outs: - Joint products are not by-products. Joint costs are allocated on a rational and consistent basis, not deducted the way by-product

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: The Case Scenario pattern in this chapter is built on manshifts, where one shift per day per employee is assumed. Manshift, EMS and OMS: \text{Manshift} = \text{No. of employees} \times \text{No. of days worked} \text{EMS} = \frac{\text{Total Employee Benefits Paid}}{\text{Manshift}} \text{OMS} = \frac{\text{Total Output}}{\text{Manshift}} \text{COP per Manshift} = \frac{\text{COP}}{\text{Total Manshift}} EMS is the cost-based ratio and OMS is the output-based ratio — the pair is easy to invert under pressure. For per-unit figures, the denominator changes with the stage: Cost per unit: \text{Cost per unit} = \frac{\text{Total cost at that stage}}{\text{Units (produced or sold, as applicable)}} COP and COGS per unit are usually computed on units produced; administration and selling overhead per unit are often computed on units sold. This is a recurring pattern rather than a fixed rule, so

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: read the requirement. There are no fixed cost-component percentage benchmarks in this chapter — the numericals are entirely data-specific. Reverse-calculation problems are a favourite: work backwards from COGS or COS using the given ratios (for example, Factory OH stated as a percentage of Direct Labour) to arrive at Prime Cost, then raw material consumed, then purchases. Treating COGS and Cost of Sales as the same thing — COGS is COP adjusted for FG stock only; COS adds general Admin OH, Selling OH, Secondary Packing, Distribution OH and the separate interest line. Stopping at Works Cost and calling it Cost of Production — COP still needs QC, process R&D, production-related Admin OH, less recoveries, plus Primary Packing. Applying the WIP adjustment to Prime Cost or to COP — it belongs strictly between Gross Works Cost and Works Cost. Putting Secondary packing in COP or Primary packing

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: in COS — essential-to-preserve packing is COP, storage/transport/promotion packing is COS. Merging the two kinds of Admin OH — production-related goes to COP, general management goes to COS. Classifying a special frame made for a specific order as material or factory OH — it is a Direct Expense; conversely the plant supervisor's salary is Factory OH, not a direct expense. Adding scrap realisation or by-product NRV as income instead of deducting both from COP — and forgetting that scrap is residual waste while a by-product is a secondary product with market value. Confusing functional classification (Production / Admin / Selling / Distribution / R&D — the basis of the cost sheet) with element classification (Material / Labour / Expenses — within Prime Cost).

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Recite the ladder cold. — DM+DL+DE = Prime Cost → +Factory OH = Gross Works Cost → ±WIP = Works Cost → +QC +R&D(process) +Admin OH(prod) −Recoveries +Primary Packing = COP → ±FG = COGS → +Admin OH(Gen) +Selling +Secondary Packing +Distribution (+Interest) = COS → Sales − COS = Profit. Three stock adjustments, three points? — RM before Prime Cost; WIP between Gross Works Cost and Works Cost; FG between COP and COGS. Packing split? — Primary (essential to hold/preserve) → COP. Secondary (storage/transport/promotion) → COS. Admin OH split? — Production-related → COP. General (Finance/GM) → COS. Where does interest go? — Never in COP, never inside Admin OH — always a separate line item at the COS stage (or shown separately in the P&L). What is excluded from the cost sheet altogether? — Abnormal costs; penalty, fine, damages, demurrage; ITC-eligible GST and duties on raw material. What is alw

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: ays deducted from COP? — Credit for recoveries (scrap/waste realisable value) and by-product NRV. Treatment of a subsidy or grant? — Reduced from the relevant cost object — not shown as income. Materials consumed formula? — Opening RM + Purchases − Closing RM; add freight-in and procurement insurance, deduct trade discount, add duty/tax only if ITC is not available. Manshift, EMS, OMS? — Manshift = Employees × Days worked. EMS = Total employee benefits ÷ Manshift. OMS = Total output ÷ Manshift. Per-unit denominators? — COP and COGS per unit → units produced. Admin OH and Selling OH per unit → often units sold. MCQ trap round: classify each. — Special frame = Direct Expense · supervisor / store staff / canteen = Factory OH · lab and QC staff = QC Cost · director's laptop depreciation and audit fees = Admin OH · royalty on production = Direct Expense.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Employee cost = wages + allowances + incentives + overtime + employer PF + other benefits, in cash or kind — split into direct (traceable to a cost object) and indirect (overheads). Time-keeping records total attendance, time-booking splits it job-wise; the reconciliation is Job time + Idle time = Attendance time. Idle time: normal goes into cost of production / the overhead rate, abnormal goes to the Costing P&L and is further split controllable / uncontrollable. Overtime = normal wages + premium, and the premium's treatment depends entirely on the CAUSE — customer, general production, another department's fault, or abnormal conditions. Halsey pays 50% of time saved, Rowan pays the (TS/SH) proportion; turnover uses Replacement, Separation and Flux methods, all over the same denominator — average employees on roll.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: The whole chapter runs in one sequence — mnemonic "ATTIRE-OWNS": Attendance/Payroll → Time-keeping vs Time-booking → Idle Time → Overtime → Wage Systems (Time / Piece / Halsey / Rowan) → Night shift & Absorption → Summary (Efficiency + Turnover + Direct Expenses). Employee cost: Benefits paid or payable to employees — permanent or temporary, in cash or in kind . It is wages + allowances + incentives + overtime + employer's PF contribution + other benefits, not just the wage line. Employee cost control: Keeping wages per unit of output low. It is not minimising the total wage bill or any individual employee's wage — a higher-paid but more productive worker can mean better control. Employee cost splits two ways: direct employee cost is attributable to a cost object where economically feasible and varies positively with volume; indirect employee cost cannot be directly attributed and may no

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: t vary with volume, so it travels through overheads. Control chain: Personnel → Engineering / Work Study → Time-keeping → Payroll → Cost Accounting. Time-keeping = total attendance record; time-booking = job-wise break-up of that time. Reconciliation: Job time + Idle time = Attendance time. Wage analysis sheet analyses wages by cost centre / job / work order — it is not the payroll, which is about disbursement.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Idle time: Time paid for but not booked to any job — no output against it. The trap is to think idle time is unpaid; it is paid, which is exactly why it must be costed somewhere. passages.text: The two base systems are straight time rate (time worked × rate — "time worked" includes the normal idle period) and straight piece rate (units × rate per unit — independent of time taken, and with no guaranteed minimum wage unless separately provided). Barth is the one exception — the only premium bonus method where the day wage is not guaranteed (named only in the source, not elaborated). passages.doc: Introduction to Cost and Management Accounting
passages.subject: cma
passages.text: One widening ladder holds the chapter together: Cost → Costing → Cost Accounting → Cost Accountancy. Management accounting is wider still — qualitative plus quantitative, with no fixed rules. Five objectives of cost accounting (A-P-C-R-D): ascertain cost, determine selling price and profitability, cost control, cost reduction, decision making. Cost object (what), cost unit (measure), cost centre (where cost is accumulated), cost driver (why) — then the responsibility-centre ladder Cost → Revenue → Profit → Investment. Cost is classified on six bases — nature/element, function, variability, controllability, normality and managerial decision making — and the same cost can sit under all six at once. Methods of costing follow the industry (process = sugar, contract = real estate, operating = hospitals); techniques such as marginal, standard and absorption costing sit on top of the method.

passages.doc: Introduction to Cost and Management Accounting
passages.subject: cma
passages.section: The widening ladder — cost to cost accountancy
passages.text: Every term in this chapter sits on one widening ladder: Cost → Costing → Cost Accounting → Cost Accountancy (the "C-C-CA-CA" ladder). Each rung is wider than the one before it, and cost accountancy is the broadest of the four. Cost: A resource given up for goods or services. It works both as a noun (an amount, actual or notional) and as a verb (the act of ascertaining). A cost can be notional — no cash outlay is required for something to be a cost. Cost Accounting: Begins with the recording of income and expenditure and ends with periodical statements and reports for ascertaining and controlling cost. The exact start and end points are what gets tested. Costing (CIMA) is narrower — the technique and process of ascertaining costs. Cost Accountancy: The broadest term: costing + cost accounting + cost control + ascertainment of profitability + presentation of information for decision making

passages.doc: Introduction to Cost and Management Accounting

passages.text: . Do not equate it with mere "cost accounting". Management Accounting (CIMA): The application of accounting and financial management principles to create, protect, preserve and increase value for stakeholders. Wider than cost accounting, and bound by no fixed rules or format. Alongside these sits cost management — the application of management accounting concepts to plan, monitor and control costs. It is the umbrella over cost control and cost reduction, which are its outcomes. Cost and management accounting is itself positioned as an application of financial management. The five objectives of cost accounting follow in order — mnemonic "Ascertain Price, Control & Reduce, Decide" (A-P-C-R-D): Ascertainment of cost → Determination of selling price and profitability → Cost control → Cost reduction → Decision making . passages.section: Cost control, cost reduction and cost management
passages.text: Cost control runs as a four-step loop: set the standard → measure actual performance → compare actual with standard → analyse the variance and act on it. Cost Reduction: A real and permanent reduction in unit cost without impairing the suitability or quality of the product. Its three assumptions must all hold: there is a saving in unit cost, the saving is permanent, and quality/utility is unaffected. The tool used for cost reduction is Value Chain Analysis (Porter) — it identifies value-added against non-value-added activities. Cost leadership, meaning the lowest cost with quality maintained to give a pricing edge, is one of Porter's three generic strategies; the other two are product differentiation and focus/niche. passages.section: Cost objects, units, centres and drivers
passages.text: Four terms answer four different questions — Object-Unit-Centre-Driver = What-Measure-Where-Why: Cost object — anything needing separate cost measurement; it is the base for the direct/indirect classification. Cost unit — the unit of product, service or time used to measure cost; a physical measure, and industry-specific. Cost centre — the organisational location where cost is accumulated and controlled. Cost driver — the causal factor behind the cost. Cost Driver: A factor or activity that influences the level of cost — the ABC linkage. Examples: the number of purchase orders, the number of machine set-ups. In activity based costing the cost driver is the basis of apportionment, because ABC assigns cost to activities , not to products directly. passages.section: Classification of cost — the six bases
passages.text: Mnemonic "N-F-V-C-N-M" — Never Forget Variability, Control, Normality, MDM. The six bases are not mutually exclusive: a single cost element can be classified under all six at once. 1. Nature / element — material, labour, other expenses and overheads, each split into direct and indirect. Overheads = indirect material + indirect labour + indirect expenses. 2. Function — production, administration, selling, distribution, R&D. This drives the cost sheet flow. 3. Variability — fixed, variable, semi-variable (the semi-variable part must be segregated). 4. Controllability — controllable (influenced by a manager's action) against uncontrollable (not influenced by the specified individual, e.g. tool-room cost apportioned to the machine shop). Always relative. 5. Normality — normal cost, incurred at the given/normal output level, against abnormal cost, which is charged to the Costing P&L Account a

passages.text: Five methods segregate a semi-variable cost. The least squares method is statistically the best per ICAI; the graphical method is the most subjective and judgmental — plot output on X against cost on Y, fit a line of best fit, read fixed cost off the Y-intercept, and take variable cost as total less fixed. passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Job costing is a specific order costing method — the job is the cost unit, authorised by a customer's specific order with its own specifications (CIMA London definition). Batch costing is the same logic with the batch as the cost unit; the cost unit is the only difference. Each job carries its own cost sheet: material, then labour, with overheads added on completion — flowing through Bill of Material, Stores Requisition, Job Time Card and Standing Order numbers. Overheads are apportioned to departments, re-apportioned from service to production, then absorbed on a base (machine hour, labour hour, % wages, % material) — different bases give a different job cost, so absorption is inherently arbitrary. Spoiled work cannot be rectified, defective work can; compare actual against the normal rate — normal goes to the job or batch, abnormal is always written off to the Costing P&L A/c.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Mnemonic — "Job Says: My Cost Order Accounted". The chain is: Methods of Costing → Specific Order Costing → Job Costing → cost collection (M-L-OH) → overheads and spoilage → accounting through control accounts. Job Cost Sheet — the format, one per job. Collect costs — Material + Labour + Overheads. Spoiled / Defective work — three circumstances, three treatments. Control A/c entries — thirteen journal entries. Job Costing (CIMA London): The basic costing method applicable where work consists of separate contracts, jobs or batches , each of which is authorised by a specific order . Always attribute the definition to CIMA London — the source is what students forget. Job: A specific order with its own specifications , treated as a separate cost unit . This is what separates it from process costing, which is continuous and homogeneous. Batch Costing: Identical logic to job costing — the only

Process of job costing: a cost sheet is opened per job → material cost is charged → labour cost is charged → overheads are added on completion. Where it suits: different customers, no two orders alike, and work-in-progress varying with the jobs in hand. Features to recall: a separate cost sheet per job; work done against the customer's specific order and specifications; no two jobs alike; WIP varies with jobs in hand; costs ascertained on completion; and more managerial control needed because production is non-continuous. passages.text: Define job costing — and whose definition is it? — CIMA London: the basic costing method applicable where work consists of separate contracts, jobs or batches, each authorised by a specific order. Labour document flow? — Job Time Card → Labour Abstract Book → WIP Ledger; idle time and indirect labour go to the Overhead Ledger instead. passages.subject: cma
passages.text: The split-off point is the pivot of the whole chapter — everything spent up to it is joint cost (which must be apportioned), everything after it is further processing cost (directly allocated, never apportioned). Joint products carry equal importance and significant sale value each; by-products are incidental with insignificant value; co-products are contemporary but need not share the same material or process. Seven methods apportion joint cost — mnemonic PN-TMA-C: Physical Units, NRV at split-off, Technical Estimates, then Market value at separation, Market value after processing, Average Unit Cost and Contribution Margin. By-products have four valuation methods (NRV, Standard Cost, Comparative Price, Re-use Basis) and three accounting treatments, picked by whether the value is small, considerable, or depends on further processing. Sell-at-split-off versus process-further is settled by incremental revenue against incremental cost, product by product — the apportioned joint cost is sunk and irrelevant.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: One common process, one common pool of cost, several saleable outputs — and no engineering way to say which rupee belongs to which product. That is the entire problem of this chapter, and every question is a variation on it. Learn it as a pipeline: Classify the outputs — joint products, by-products or co-products → Locate the split-off point — the moment the products become separately identifiable → Cost up to split-off = joint cost → apportion it by one of the seven methods → Cost after split-off = further processing cost → allocate it directly to the product that caused it → By-products → value them (four methods) and route them into one of three accounting treatments → Decide sell-or-process-further on incremental figures alone. The apportionment methods have a mnemonic — PN-TMA-C: Physical Units → NRV at split-off → Technical Estimates (these three are the "commonly used" set) → Mark

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: et value (at separation, or after further processing) → Average unit cost → Contribution margin (these last four are the managerial-decision methods).

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Joint products: Two or more products of equal importance , produced simultaneously from the same process , each with a significant relative sale value . No single product is the "major" one — e.g. gasoline, fuel oil and kerosene from crude petroleum. By-products: Products recovered incidentally from the discarded material or scrap of a main process, of relatively insignificant value compared with the main product — e.g. molasses from sugar, glycerin from soap, and tar, ammonia and benzole from coal. Co-products: Contemporary products that are not necessarily produced from the same material or process — e.g. wheat and gram grown on separate farms, or timber from different trees. Co-products can themselves have by-products (a favourite MCQ trap). Split-off point: The point at which the joint products and by-products become separately identifiable . Joint cost runs only up to this point; ev

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: erything after it is product-specific. Joint cost: Expenditure incurred up to the split-off point on the common input — material, labour, power, fuel, depreciation and overheads. The apportionment problem exists only for this cost. Further processing cost (post split-off cost) is incurred after split-off on an individual product. It is directly allocable and product-specific, and is never apportioned. passages.subject: cma
passages.section: Apportioning joint cost to joint products
passages.text: Physical Units Method: \text{Cost to a product} = \frac{\text{Physical units of that product}}{\text{Total physical units}} \times \text{Total Joint Cost} Convert every output to a common unit first. Process loss or wastage is also apportioned over the products on the same physical (weight) ratio. If the outputs cannot be reduced to a common unit of measurement, the method is simply inapplicable. NRV at Split-off Method: \text{NRV} = \text{Sales Value (after processing)} - \text{Profit Margin (if any)} - \text{S\&D Expenses} - \text{Post split-off Cost} \text{Cost to a product} = \frac{\text{NRV of that product}}{\text{Total NRV}} \times \text{Total Joint Cost} All three deductions are possible in the full pro-forma — do not stop at the further processing cost. Technical Estimates has no formula at all: engineers and technical experts judge the apportionment directly. Use it when the NRV

Market Value at Split-off (Multiplying Factor): \text{Multiplying Factor} = \frac{\text{Joint Cost}}{\text{Total Sales Revenue}} \times 100 \text{Cost to a product} = \text{Sales revenue of that product} \times \text{Multiplying Factor} The same answer can be reached by apportioning joint cost directly in the ratio of sales value at split-off. Market Value after Further Processing: \text{Cost to a product} = \frac{\text{Market sales value after processing of that product}}{\text{Total market sales value after processing}} \times \text{Total Joint Cost} This method is unfair and invalid when further processing costs are disproportionate, or when not all products are processed further — switch to the NRV method in those cases. Contribution Margin Method: \text{Variable cost to a product} = \frac{\text{Physical quantity of that product}}{\text{Total physical quantity}} \times \text{Total Variable Cost} \text{Contribution} = \text{Sales} - \text{Total Variable Cost} \text{Fixed cost to a product} = \frac{\text{Contribution of that product}}{\text{Total Contribution}} \times \text{Total Fixed Cost} Variable cost goes by units, fixed cost by the contribution ratio — the two bases must never be swapped. Three situations decide the accounting treatment: (a) Small total value — either credit the sale value to the Costing P&L A/c as miscellaneous or other income (no credit in the cost accounts), or deduct the sale proceeds from total cost (production cost or cost of sales). Never apply both at once — that double-counts. (b) Considerable value — treat the by-product as a joint product : apportion the cost up to split-off by relative market value, physical output or ultimate selling price. (c) Needs further processing — first find NRV at split-off = rea

passages.subject: cma
passages.section: Sell at split-off or process further
passages.text: Incremental analysis: \text{Incremental Profit} = (\text{Sales after processing} - \text{Sales at split-off}) - \text{Incremental further processing cost} Process further only if incremental profit is positive; otherwise sell at split-off. Three rules carry every question of this type: Compare incremental revenue (sales value after processing − sales value at split-off) with incremental cost (the further processing cost) — nothing else enters. The apportioned or joint cost is sunk . It is irrelevant to the decision and must not be included in the incremental statement — the single most common student error here. Decide per product, independently . The classic exam pattern is a multi-product statement in which some products show incremental profit (process further) and others an incremental loss (sell at split-off) — the answer is the optimal mix , not one uniform decision.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Situation in the data Method to use --- --- Selling price is uniform across products Physical Units Split-off value is not known NRV at split-off Split-off value known, but further processing costs are disproportionate Market value at separation Further processing costs proportionate and all products processed further Market value after further processing Financial data unreliable Technical Estimates Cost behaviour (variable vs fixed) needs to be reflected Contribution Margin Dragging the apportioned joint cost into the sell-or-process-further statement — it is sunk and irrelevant; only incremental revenue and incremental cost matter. Taking one uniform decision for all products in a further-processing question — decide product by product and report the optimal combination. Apportioning post split-off cost — it is directly allocable and product-specific, and is never apportioned. Mnemonic: PN-TMA-C. Four by-product apportionment methods? — NRV Method; Standard Cost / Technical Estimates; Comparative Price; Re-use Basis. passages.subject: cma
passages.text: One master equation drives the whole chapter: S − V = C = F ± P. Every other formula here is a transformation of it — 17 variations in all. The golden chain runs Marginal Cost → Contribution → P/V Ratio → BEP → Margin of Safety → Angle of Incidence. Learn it in that order and nothing has to be memorised twice. P/V ratio is a function of selling price per unit and variable cost per unit ONLY — it never moves with volume or with fixed cost. Short-term decisions use controllable + relevant costs only: historical, sunk and committed costs are always irrelevant; opportunity and shutdown costs are always relevant, notional cost only conditionally. Marginal and absorption profit differ purely because of stock: closing greater than opening → absorption profit higher; opening greater than closing → marginal profit higher.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Four blocks, in this order — mnemonic "M-CVP-A-D": Marginal cost basics → CVP analysis → Application in decisions → Distinction between marginal and absorption costing. 1. Foundations — marginal cost, marginal costing, direct costing, differential and incremental cost, contribution, period cost, absorption costing as the contrast (with 7 advantages and 7 limitations of the technique). 2. CVP analysis — the chain "E-A-I-M-B-V-A" : Equation (S−V=C=F±P) → P/V Ratio → BEP in units and value → Cash BEP → Multi-product BEP → Margin of Safety → Angle of Incidence, plus three charts. 3. Application in decisions — "controllable + relevant only": the relevance filter, then excess-supply decisions and excess-demand decisions. 4. MC vs AC distinction — valuation basis, treatment of fixed cost, profit under four stock scenarios, and the two income-statement formats. The golden chain to recite before

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: the exam: Marginal Cost → Contribution → P/V Ratio → BEP → MoS → Angle of Incidence. All of them derive from the master equation, which appears in 17 variations.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Marginal cost: The incremental cost of ONE additional unit — the total variable cost attributable to that unit. It is not the same as an incremental or batch cost: a machine set-up of ₹1,200 is a batch cost, not the marginal cost of one unit. Marginal costing: A technique , not a distinct costing method like job or process costing. Products and inventory are valued at variable cost only , and every fixed cost is treated as a period cost . Direct costing is a synonym — though a direct cost is not always a marginal cost (batch, product and department-level costs exist). Contribution: Sales − Total Variable Cost. On the "joint cost" theory it is a single fund that first covers fixed cost and then becomes profit — so contribution can be positive while profit is still negative. On period cost vs product cost: under marginal costing all fixed costs — manufacturing and non-manufacturing alike —

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: are period costs, charged to the P&L of the period. Product (inventoriable) cost is variable manufacturing cost only; variable selling and distribution overhead is not a product cost and is deducted after Product Contribution Margin. Two neighbouring concepts that examiners deliberately blur: - Differential cost — the difference between the costs of two given production levels (a comparison). - Incremental cost — the increase in cost caused by a change in volume or process (directional, cause-based). It may cover one unit or a whole volume change, which is the thin line against marginal cost. Absorption costing, the contrast throughout, charges all costs — fixed and variable — to the product on a functional classification, and therefore suffers over- and under-absorption.

passages.section: CVP analysis — the master equation and the P/V ratio
passages.text: CVP analysis is a cost-volume-profit relationship tool used for profit planning. It rests on six assumptions — among them linearity, a single cost driver, a constant sales mix, and no time value of money. Marginal cost equation (master): S - V = C = F \pm P C = S - V \qquad C = F + P S = Sales, V = Variable Cost, C = Contribution, F = Fixed Cost, P = Profit. At BEP profit is zero, so C = F. P/V ratio: \text{P/V Ratio} = \frac{C}{S} \times 100 = \frac{S - V}{S} \times 100 \text{P/V Ratio} = \frac{\Delta C \text{ or } \Delta P}{\Delta S} \times 100 S = \frac{C}{\text{P/V Ratio}} \qquad C = S \times \text{P/V Ratio} The P/V ratio is a function of selling price per unit and variable cost per unit only. It is unaffected by volume and by fixed cost. Change Effect on P/V ratio --- --- Same % increase in SP and VC UNCHANGED Increase in SP only (VC constant) INCREASES Decrease in VC only (SP cons

passages.text: Every decision passes two gates, in order. Controllability and relevance: Controllability (first gate) — the cost or benefit arises because of the choice of option. Relevance (second gate) — the cost is a future cost and it differs between options ; both conditions are needed. A cost can be controllable and still irrelevant — raw material costing the same under make and under buy, for instance. Cost type Status in a decision --- --- Historical / Sunk / Committed Always IRRELEVANT — already incurred or pre-agreed, cannot be changed Opportunity cost RELEVANT — benefit forgone from the best rejected alternative Notional / Imputed cost (e.g. notional interest) RELEVANT ONLY IF a benefit is actually being forgone (conditional) Shut-down cost RELEVANT — discretionary fixed cost avoided on suspending operations Opportunity cost, key factor and cost indifference: \text{Profitability} = \frac{\te

Limiting (key) factor: Anything that limits activity. On the supply side, the 4 M's — Men, Material, Machine, Money — and demand can limit too. Products are ranked by Contribution ÷ Key Factor , never by contribution per unit alone. Excess supply (spare capacity) decisions and excess demand (scarce resource) decisions use the same relevance filter but different rules. Step 2 — compute contribution per unit of the scarce resource (contribution ÷ key-factor usage per unit). passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Marginal costing puts only variable cost into the product and into stock, treats fixed cost as a period cost, and judges profitability through the P/V ratio. Absorption costing puts both fixed and variable cost into the product and stock, apportions fixed cost to each unit, and judges profitability through net cost per unit. Because the two techniques differ only in where fixed cost sits, the profit difference is purely stock-driven. Stock position Profit comparison --- --- No opening or closing stock EQUAL under both Opening = Closing stock EQUAL (if the fixed-cost element in both is the same) Closing greater than Opening (Production exceeds Sales) Absorption profit HIGHER — fixed cost locked into closing stock is carried forward Opening greater than Closing (Production less than Sales) Marginal profit HIGHER — last period's fixed cost in opening stock is released this period under abso

Always adjust for over/under-absorption of fixed overheads in the absorption costing statement — the commonest omission. Marginal costing income statement format: Sales → less Variable Cost → Contribution → less Fixed Cost → Profit. Absorption costing income statement format: fixed overhead sits inside cost of production (absorbed at a pre-determined rate), with a separate over/under-absorption adjustment line. Treating marginal cost as an incremental or batch cost — marginal cost is the change in cost for one extra unit (a ₹1,200 set-up is a batch cost). And differential cost is the difference between two given production levels, while incremental cost is the increase caused by a change. Using tota

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: The master equation? — S − V = C = F ± P. Every other formula in the chapter is a transposition of it. P/V ratio — all three forms? — (C ÷ S) × 100 = (S − V) ÷ S × 100 = (change in C or P) ÷ (change in S) × 100. What can change the P/V ratio? — Only a change in selling price per unit or variable cost per unit — never volume, never fixed cost. BEP — units, value and cash? — Units = Fixed Cost ÷ Contribution p.u. Value = (Total FC ÷ Contribution) × Sales = Total FC ÷ P/V Ratio. Cash BEP = Cash Fixed Cost ÷ Contribution p.u. — excludes depreciation and other non-cash fixed costs, so always lower in units. Multi-product BEP? — Common FC ÷ Composite Contribution p.u., where composite = Σ(Contribution p.u. × sales-mix weight); then split by the mix ratio. Margin of safety — two routes? — Actual/Projected Sales − Break-even Sales, or the shortcut Profit ÷ P/V Ratio. Three P/V-ratio identities?

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Follow the chapter as one flow — mnemonic PROVE-I: Procurement → Receipt Valuation → Organize/Store → Verify/Control Inventory → Exit (Issue + Pricing) → losses and consumption. Receipt valuation: add duty, freight, insurance and brokerage; deduct trade/quantity discount and subsidy; cash discount is always IGNORED. Three stores records, three owners: Bin Card (qty, storekeeper) · Stock Control Card (qty, central) · Stores Ledger (qty + value, cost department). Inventory control rests on EOQ = √(2AO/C) — at EOQ, ordering cost equals carrying cost — plus ROL, minimum, maximum, average and danger levels, and the ABC/FSN/VED/HML classifications. Loss rule NAP: Normal loss is Absorbed by good units, Abnormal loss goes to the Costing P&L A/c. Obsolescence is ALWAYS abnormal.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Material cost is one long pipeline, and every question in this chapter sits somewhere on it. Learn the order once — mnemonic PROVE-I: P — Procurement : BOM → Purchase Requisition → RFP/NIT (L1) → Purchase Order → GRN / Material Returned Note → Bill passing. R — Receipt Valuation : add duty, freight, insurance, brokerage; deduct trade discount, quantity discount, subsidy; cash discount ignored. O — Organize/Store : Bin Card, Stock Control Card, Stores Ledger. V — Verify/Control Inventory : stock levels, ABC/FSN/VED/HML, ratios, physical control systems. E — Exit (Issue + Pricing) : cost prices, average prices, market prices, notional prices. I — Losses and consumption : waste, scrap, spoilage, defectives, obsolescence. Direct material: Cost directly attributable to the end product where tracing is economically feasible . Trap: material that is traceable but where tracing is not economical

passages.section: Inventory control — EOQ and stock levels
passages.text: Economic Order Quantity (EOQ): The order size that minimises the total of ordering cost and carrying cost . Trap: EOQ does not minimise the purchase price. Ordering cost covers quotations, documentation, transport and inspection; carrying cost covers funds, storage, insurance and obsolescence. EOQ — mnemonic 2AO/C: \text{EOQ} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2AO}{C}} Where $A$ = annual usage in units, $O$ = ordering cost per order, and $C$ = carrying cost per unit per annum. At EOQ, ordering cost = carrying cost. \text{Number of orders per year} = \dfrac{\text{Annual Consumption}}{\text{EOQ}} \text{Total Variable Cost at order size } Q = \text{Purchase Cost} + \dfrac{A}{Q} \times O + \dfrac{Q}{2} \times C Here $\frac{A}{Q} \times O$ is the ordering cost and $\frac{Q}{2} \times C$ is the carrying cost. Buffer/safety stock is proactive — a cushion for sudden or unexpected demand, held in excess of lead-time consumption. ### Two special cases that break the plain formula EOQ with quantity discount : compute total cost (purchase + ordering + carrying) at the EOQ level and at each discount slab's order size, then pick the order size with the least total cost . The answer may not be the mathematical EOQ. Physical contro

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: l sits alongside the records: Two Bin System — the bin is split into a reserve portion (equal to the minimum level / ROL) and an issue portion; it supplements the Bin Card and Stores Ledger. Perpetual Inventory — the continuous record system of Bin Card + Stores Ledger, so quantity and value are available at any time without waiting for a stock-take. Continuous Stock Verification — ongoing, surprise physical checking by internal audit (independent), as against an annual stock-take that halts production. Method How it works Trap / keyword --- --- --- FIFO Earliest lot issued first Good in falling prices; closing stock ≈ market price LIFO Latest lot issued first Not permitted under AS-2 / Ind AS-2 — academic only Base Stock Minimum reserve carried at the first lot's original cost; the rest priced by FIFO or LIFO A dependent method, never independent Simple Average Average of unit prices of lots — quantity ignored Exclude the rate of a lot that is fully exhausted; distorted if lot sizes vary Weighted Average Average weighted by the quantity of each lot Recomputed on every fresh receipt, not on every issue Standard Price Predetermined rate; judges purchase department efficiency Hard to fix when prices swing widely Repla

It is not a general rule.

passages.text: The single rule that covers all five loss types — mnemonic NAP: Normal loss is Absorbed by good units; abnormal loss goes to the Costing P&L A/c. Obsolescence: Loss arising from supersession or technological advancement. It is a total loss and ALWAYS abnormal , with no exceptions — never part of the cost of manufacture; dispose of the item at the best price obtainable. Loss type Normal Abnormal --- --- --- Shortage Absorbed by good units — raises effective cost per unit Debited to Costing P&L A/c; excluded from product cost Waste Absorbed by good production (inherent) Costing P&L A/c (avoidable/controllable) Scrap Cost borne by good units; realisable value credited/deducted (net cost adjustment) Scrap A/c charged with full cost, job/process credited; profit or loss on realisation → Costing P&L Spoilage Charged to the production order or spread via overhead; realised value credited back C

High ratio = fast-moving; low ratio = capital locked up. ABC vs FSN vs VED vs HML? — ABC = value-based; FSN = turnover-based; VED = criticality-based (spares); HML = unit-cost-based. Spoilage vs defectives? — Spoilage ca

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Overheads are indirect costs that cannot be conveniently traced to a cost unit — classified by function, nature, element and control. The whole chapter is one pipeline: Estimate → Allocate → Apportion (primary) → Re-apportion (secondary) → Absorb, then compare absorbed with actual. Allocation charges a WHOLE item to one department; apportionment splits a PROPORTION across many departments using a base. Service department costs come back to production departments by direct redistribution, the step method, or a reciprocal method (simultaneous equation, trial and error, repeated distribution). Absorbed less than actual is under-absorption (debit balance); the treatment turns on whether the gap is small, an estimation error, or abnormal.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Overheads are the costs left over once direct material, direct labour and direct expenses have been traced. Because they cannot be traced, they must be pushed to cost units through a fixed sequence. Learn the sequence first — every numerical in this chapter is one step of it. E-A-A-R-A — Estimate → Allocate → Apportion → Re-apportion → Absorb. 1. Estimation and collection — overhead heads are collected against standing orders . 2. Allocation — the whole item of cost goes to one department (direct). 3. Apportionment (primary distribution) — a proportion of the item is split across many departments through a base (indirect). 4. Re-apportionment (secondary distribution) — service department costs are pushed onto production departments. 5. Absorption — production department cost is recovered from cost units through an overhead absorption rate (blanket or departmental). 6. Compare absorbed ag

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: ainst actual → under/over-absorption → supplementary rate or Costing P&L A/c. Overheads: Expenditure not conveniently traceable to a cost unit, incurred for output generally. The trap: overheads are not only factory costs — administration, selling and distribution overheads count too. Overheads are classified four different ways, and an exam question can ask for any of them: Classification basis Classes --- --- Function Factory/production, administration, selling, distribution Nature (behaviour) Fixed, variable, semi-variable Element Indirect material, indirect labour, indirect expenses Control Controllable, uncontrollable Each functional class has its own boundary, and the boundaries are where marks are lost: - Factory/production OH — indirect cost from material procurement through to the finished product; includes primary packing and production-related administration. - Administration

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: OH — general management, policy and direction cost, not tied to production, selling or R&D. On a finance lease, only the rental (excluding the finance cost) is included. - Selling OH — cost of promoting marketing and sale: salesmen's commission, advertisement. - Distribution OH — cost of making the product available in the market: delivery van, secondary packing. Two behavioural rules govern absorption throughout the chapter: variable overheads are absorbed on actual production, fixed overheads on normal capacity.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Cost allocation: Direct assignment of a whole item of cost to one cost centre. It is the wider term — allocation is possible whenever the expense belongs entirely to one centre. Cost apportionment: Distribution of a proportion of an item of cost among several departments. An indirect process — it always needs a base . Standing order: A sanction number allotted to an indirect expense head for collection purposes. Standing orders are used for overheads only — never for direct material or direct labour. Whether a cost is allocated or apportioned depends on the relationship between the expense and the cost centre, not on the nature of the expense itself. ### Bases of apportionment — primary distribution Overhead Base --- --- Rent, lighting, heating, air-conditioning, fire precaution Floor area / volume Welfare, time-keeping, personnel, supervision Number of workers Compensation, holiday pay,

passages.text: The overhead sequence in five steps? — Estimate → Allocate → Apportion (primary) → Re-apportion (secondary) → Absorb. Then compare absorbed with actual. Allocation vs apportionment? — Allocation = whole item, direct, to one department. Apportionment = a proportion of the item split across many departments on a base. Which base absorbs fixed overheads? And variable? — Fixed overheads on normal capacity; variable overheads on actual production. Name the reciprocal service methods. — Simultaneous equation (algebraic, exact), trial and error (iterative, same answer), repeated distribution (iterative to service and production departments, converges to the same result). Where does the step method start? — With the service department serving the maximum number of other departments; distribute sequentially, and the last department's cost goes to production departments only. passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Process costing applies where there are two or more sequential processes, the output of one becoming the input of the next; output is homogeneous and cost is averaged over units. One golden formula runs the whole chapter: cost per unit = (Total Cost − Realisable Value of Normal Loss) ÷ (Input Units − Normal Loss Units) — and the SAME rate values good output, abnormal loss and abnormal gain. Normal loss is absorbed by good units with no P&L effect; abnormal loss is credited out of the Process A/c to Costing P&L; abnormal gain is debited into the Process A/c and mirrors abnormal loss. Work-in-progress is valued through equivalent units computed element-wise (material, labour, overhead) — FIFO uses current-period cost only, weighted average blends opening WIP cost with current cost. Inter-process profit transfers output at market value or cost plus a percentage: Transfer Price = (Total Cost − Closing Stock) ÷ (1 − profit % on TP), stock is valued at prime cost, and unrealised profit is stripped out. Operation costing is the hybrid of job costing for material and process costing for conversion.

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Process costing is used where production runs through two or more sequential processes, the output of one process becoming the input of the next, the output is homogeneous, and cost is averaged over the units produced. Costs do not attach to an identifiable job — the product loses its identity in a continuous flow. Learn the chapter as a single sequence — mnemonic "MC-TVS-PIO": M eaning → C osting procedure → T reatment of loss / gain → V aluation of WIP through equivalent units → S teps 1–5: physical flow → equivalent units → total cost → cost per EU → assign cost → P rocess methods (FIFO / weighted average) → I nter-process profit → O peration costing. The costing procedure itself is simple bookkeeping: material + labour + direct expenses + overhead are charged to each Process Account, and the output value is carried forward to the next process. Everything numerical in this chapter gro

passages.text: ws out of one expression. Memorise it before anything else: Cost per unit (good output) — the golden formula: \text{Cost per unit} = \frac{\text{Total Cost} - \text{Realisable Value of Normal Loss}}{\text{Input Units} - \text{Normal Loss Units}} Process costing: Costs are charged to processes and averaged over the units produced, across two or more sequential processes. Contrast with job costing: here the product loses its identity in a continuous flow, so cost cannot be traced to a specific job. Where indirect expenses are common to several processes, the source uses wages as the apportionment base: Apportionment of indirect expenses: \text{Indirect expense of a process} = \frac{\text{Total Indirect Expenses}}{\text{Total Wages of all processes}} \times \text{Wages of that process}

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Process loss = Input quantity − Output quantity. That is an umbrella term: it covers both normal and abnormal loss, and confusing the umbrella with one of its parts is a classic slip. Normal loss: Inherent, unavoidable and anticipated loss, including quantities used up in sampling and testing. It is always computed on the estimated percentage of input, never on the actual loss, and it carries no equivalent units . Abnormal loss: Loss in excess of normal loss — caused by carelessness, bad design, sabotage and the like. It is valued at the same rate as good units , not at scrap rate. Abnormal gain (abnormal yield): Arises when actual loss is less than normal loss, because the normal loss was over-estimated or the process ran efficiently. The Process A/c is debited as if extra input had arrived, and the net amount reaches the Costing P&L only after the scrap adjustment. The value of normal

Valuing the three outcomes: \text{Value of units transferred} = \text{Cost per unit} \times \text{Units transferred} \text{Value of Abnormal Loss} = \text{Cost per unit} \times \text{Abnormal Loss Units} \text{Value of Abnormal Gain} = \text{Cost per unit} \times \text{Abnormal Gain Units} Item Treatment Key rule --- --- --- Normal loss Cost absorbed by good units; scrap value credited to Process A/c No P&L effect; if no realisable value → value = 0 Abnormal loss Credited to Process A/c (removed) → debited to Costing P&L A/c Net P&L charge = value at process rate − its own scrap realisable value Abnormal gain Process A/c debited (as if extra input) Abnormal Gain A/c: credited by Process A/c (full value); debite

passages.text: Equivalent units: Incomplete units restated as their equivalent in completed units. Computed element-wise — material, labour and overhead separately, because the percentage of completion differs by element. Normal loss carries nil equivalent units; abnormal loss and abnormal gain are always 100% . Work-in-progress — partly processed units, opening or closing — is valued through equivalent units, not through actual cost. Equivalent units and cost per equivalent unit: \text{Equivalent Units} = \text{Actual units in process} \times \text{\% of work completed} \text{Cost per Equivalent Unit} = \frac{\text{Total Cost for the element}}{\text{Equivalent Units for the element}} The cost pool feeding that second formula is where the two methods split: FIFO uses current-period cost only, while weighted average uses opening WIP cost + current cost. passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Under this system each process is treated as a separate profit centre: output is transferred to the next process at market value or cost plus a percentage, not at cost. The difference between cost and transfer price is the inter-process profit. Transfer price is the price, inclusive of profit, at which output moves to the next process. The profit percentage is stated on the transfer price, not on cost — so you divide by (1 − profit %); you never multiply. Transfer price and profit on transfer: \text{Transfer Price} = \frac{\text{Total Cost} - \text{Closing Stock}}{1 - \text{Profit \% on Transfer Price}} \text{Profit on transfer} = \text{Transfer Price} \times \text{Profit \% on TP} Stock valuation is the second half of the topic: Stock-in-process is valued at prime cost only — materials + wages + direct expenses, with no overhead and no profit . Finished stock is valued at the price rece

Both in-process and finished stock carry embedded profit , so the unrealised profit on unsold closing stock must be computed and excluded from Costing P&L until the goods are sold. Cost of closing stock (stripping unrealised profit): \text{Cost of Closing Stock} = \frac{\text{Cost element of transferred-in goods}}{\text{Transfer price of transferred-in goods}} \times \text{Value of Closing Stock (at TP)}

passages.subject: cma
passages.text: Operation costing: A hybrid system: material is costed job-wise or batch-wise, while conversion cost is costed process-wise or department-wise using a predetermined application rate (a budgeted conversion cost rate applied to products). Know the dual ICAI description for theory answers — operation costing is described both as (a) a hybrid system combining job costing for material with process costing for conversion, and (b) a "refinement of process costing" concerned with the cost of each operation rather than each process. It fits situations with multiple product variants using different materials but similar conversion — the source's examples are garments, shoes and jewellery. Process costing, by contrast, suits a single homogeneous product line. Valuing abnormal loss or abnormal gain at scrap rate — they are first valued at the process cost rate , the same rate as good units; their ow

It is always on the estimated/anticipated percentage of input, even when abnormal loss or gain has occurred. Applying the batch's overall WIP completion percentage to abnormal loss/gain units — even if the rest of the batch is 60% complete, abnormal loss and gain are 100% complete for material, labour and overhead alike. Giving normal loss equivalent units — normal loss carries nil EU. Multiplying by the profit percentage to find transfer price. Profit is on the transfer price, so you divide by (1 − profit %). Blending opening WIP into the cost pool under FIFO. FIFO uses current-period cost only ; only weighted average adds opening WIP cost. passages.subject: cma
passages.text: The golden formula? — Cost per unit = (Total Cost − Realisable Value of Normal Loss) ÷ (Input Units − Normal Loss Units). Apply the SAME rate to good output, abnormal loss and abnormal gain. Normal loss — quantity basis and P&L effect? — Always on the estimated/anticipated % of input, never on actual. Abnormal loss entries? — Credit the Process A/c (removing it), debit Costing P&L; net off any scrap realised on those units — net charge = process-rate value − own realisable value. Abnormal gain entries? — Debit the Process A/c. Abnormal Gain A/c is credited by the Process A/c (full value), debited by Normal Loss A/c (scrap value of AG units at normal-loss rate); the balance is credited to Costing P&L.
